ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding

Jaeyong Song Affiliation: Meta Affiliation: Seoul National University Work done during an internship at Meta    Daniel Wang Affiliation: Meta    Pratyush Patel Affiliation: Meta    Jonny Kong Affiliation: Meta    Preyas Shah Affiliation: Meta    Shobhit Kanaujia Affiliation: Meta
Abstract

Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. Recent systems optimize goodput (i.e., accepted tokens per second) because rejected drafts steal compute from other requests. However, these systems control only how many tokens are verified, so every request still drafts a full block. At high serving load, we find that drafting consumes up to 40% of step time, of which a majority is discarded because it is never verified. Yet, draft-length control from autoregressive drafters does not carry over, because a parallel drafter commits to its length before its single pass. Moreover, draft and verification lengths are coupled across the batch, so they must be selected jointly for every request while keeping the decision computationally cheap at every step. In this paper, we propose work-conserving speculation (WCS), a design that jointly allocates draft and verification budgets per request in LLM serving, and present ForeSpark as its prototype. ForeSpark realizes WCS with (i) a context-aware pre-draft estimator that predicts acceptance for every candidate length from the target model’s context features, (ii) a lightweight joint draft-verify scheduler that selects both lengths through a global sort, and (iii) a post-draft budget distribution that spends verification on the most promising tokens. Implemented on vLLM, ForeSpark improves throughput by up to 1.77×\times over the state-of-the-art DSpark and by 2.49×\times over autoregressive decoding at a matched per-request generation rate, without changing the output distribution. It also tolerates higher load, sustaining up to 1.51×\times the request rate of DSpark under latency service level objectives (SLOs).

2 Introduction

Speculative decoding leverages the idle compute during LLM decoding to accelerate inference (Leviathan et al., 2023; Sadhukhan et al., 2025). A drafter proposes several tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass without changing its output distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2026a).

To avoid the per-token forward passes of autoregressive drafters (e.g., MTP (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024b) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025)), parallel drafters (Chen et al., 2026a; Inco AI, 2026; Cheng et al., 2026) propose a block of KK tokens in one forward pass. Within the block, the drafter typically attends bidirectionally, so the logits for all KK positions are produced in one backbone pass.

Recent parallel drafters (Cheng et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026) optimize goodput, the number of accepted tokens per second, because under high load, verification becomes compute-bound and rejected draft tokens take compute from other requests (Sadhukhan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b). They address this through adaptive verification, which uses predicted acceptance to truncate each request’s verification to its most promising drafts. As Fig. 1(a) shows, adaptive verification (DSpark) substantially lifts throughput over full verification (DFlash2) under high load.

Adaptive verification, however, still drafts a full block of KK tokens for every request, implicitly assuming the parallel draft is computationally cheap. We find that this assumption is costly under high load. As Fig. 1(b) shows, drafting takes up to 40% of DSpark’s time per output token (gray bars). The reason is a mismatch between drafting and verification: at a load of 512 requests, adaptive verification retains only 3.77 of the 15 drafted tokens per request, while the drafter still generates all 15. Thus, 75% of the drafter’s computation is discarded, leaving LLM serving suboptimal.

A simple remedy is vLLM’s load-based batch-wise length cap (BW in Fig. 1(a)), which shortens every speculation under load and already edges out DSpark at several loads. Yet it applies one length to every request, so a better remedy is to choose the length per request, adapting approaches for autoregressive drafters (Huang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2024). However, parallel drafters differ structurally from autoregressive ones, which poses two challenges.

  1. 1.

    Draft length cannot be adjusted during drafting. Autoregressive drafters evaluate draft quality token by token and can stop as soon as their confidence drops (Huang et al., 2025a). Parallel drafters instead commit to a block size before their single pass, so they cannot prune candidates during drafting, and adaptive verification estimates acceptance only after the drafting compute is spent (Cheng et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026). Past acceptance (Li et al., 2026a) is a poor proxy (Pan et al., 2025), changing across consecutive steps in over 80% of cases (Section 4). Adaptive verification also makes this proxy unexploitable, as truncation hides the actual acceptance length.

  2. 2.

    Joint length allocation is combinatorial yet must be computationally cheap. The scheduler must jointly choose, per request, a draft length and a verification budget within one step, while keeping the decision computationally cheap. The two lengths are coupled, making the decision combinatorial, since a token never drafted cannot be verified while a surplus draft token can be dropped during verification, so the scheduler must sometimes over-draft and set both lengths together to maximize goodput.

To address these challenges, we propose work-conserving speculation (WCS), a design for jointly allocating draft and verification budgets per request in LLM serving, and build ForeSpark as its prototype. WCS organizes each draft-and-verify step into four coordinated stages, pre-draft estimate, joint schedule, draft, and distribute, so that drafting and verification compute is spent only where it pays off, the sense in which we call it work-conserving. ForeSpark realizes WCS through the following methods.

  • •

    Context-aware pre-draft estimation. We observe that the target’s context features at the last accepted token signal how predictable upcoming tokens are. Before drafting, a lightweight estimator reads them to predict acceptance for every candidate length, helping address both challenges.

  • •

    Lightweight joint scheduling. To address the combinatorial search overhead, we replace each request’s expected acceptance across candidate lengths with its concave envelope. This reduces multi-request length allocation to one global sort, so the scheduler assigns per-request draft lengths and verification budgets. When drafting is computationally cheap, the scheduler intentionally over-drafts and defers the verification decision to the post-draft stage.

  • •

    Post-draft budget distribution. A variable-length drafter executes the schedule as one packed batch, so shorter drafts save compute directly. A post-draft estimator re-scores the drafts, and the system distributes the verification budget across the batch to the most promising ones.

We implement ForeSpark on vLLM 0.30.0 (Kwon et al., 2023) and evaluate it on Qwen3-14B, GLM5.3-Flash, and GLM5.3, which span a range of model types and sizes. ForeSpark improves throughput by up to 1.77×\times over the state-of-the-art DSpark and by 2.49×\times over autoregressive decoding at a matched per-request generation rate, without changing the output distribution. As Fig. 1 previews, ForeSpark attains the highest throughput by jointly scheduling drafting and verification. It also tolerates higher load, sustaining up to 1.51×\times the request rate of DSpark under latency SLOs. Because full-block drafting with adaptive verification, as in DSpark, is a special case within ForeSpark’s design space, ForeSpark performs comparably to DSpark under low load. Since WCS is orthogonal to drafter design, it can also lift the throughput of existing parallel and autoregressive drafters (Section 7.7). We believe WCS provides a foundation for future parallel drafters in LLM serving.

3 Background

Speculative decoding. Speculative decoding generates multiple tokens per target-model pass by pairing the target with a lightweight drafter (Leviathan et al., 2023). As depicted in Fig. 2, in each step the drafter extends the anchor, the last accepted or generated token, by up to KK proposed tokens (KK=4 in the example). The target model verifies all proposals in one forward pass, accepts the longest matching prefix (e.g., A,B), and emits one bonus token (e.g., F) that becomes the next anchor. With τ\tau tokens emitted per step, throughput is τ/(Tdraft+Tverify)\tau/(T_{\mathrm{draft}}+T_{\mathrm{verify}}), so speculation pays off only when τ\tau is high and both times stay small.

Parallel speculative decoding. Autoregressive drafters (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024b) run one pass per draft position, so TdraftT_{\mathrm{draft}} grows with KK. As shown in Fig. 2, parallel drafters instead fill a block of KK mask tokens and generate all KK tokens in a single pass of a parallel backbone that attends to target-model features (Chen et al., 2026a). Within a block, bidirectional attention modestly raises acceptance over causal attention (Qian et al., 2026), but as no position sees the tokens chosen before it, later proposals can contradict earlier ones. DSpark repairs this with a sequential corrector that conditions each position on its predecessor (C→\xrightarrow{}D, D→\xrightarrow{}E) (Cheng et al., 2026), and similarly, DFlash2 addresses this with a lightweight path selector over the backbone’s top candidates (Inco AI, 2026).

Goodput-aware speculation. A serving engine batches nn requests, and each verification step processes NN non-speculative tokens (one anchor per decoding request plus prefill tokens) and BB draft tokens. Beyond some load, verification becomes compute-bound and each extra verified token lengthens the whole batch’s step, so serving systems consider goodput, the rate of accepted tokens, alongside acceptance (Sadhukhan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b).

DSpark pursues goodput with adaptive verification (Cheng et al., 2026). For request ii, its corrector estimates the probability ωi,j\omega_{i,j} that the token at draft position jj (the jj-th token after the anchor) is accepted given its predecessors, and the survival probability Si,j=∏t≤jωi,tS_{i,j}=\prod_{t\leq j}\omega_{i,t} gives the expected gain of verifying position jj (0.9, 0.72, 0.14, and 0.10 in Fig. 2). The scheduler pools Si,jS_{i,j} from all requests, sorts them so that S(r)S_{(r)} is the rr-th largest, and picks the budget

arg​maxB⁡n+∑r=1BS(r)Tdraft+Tverify​(N+B),\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{B}\frac{n+\sum_{r=1}^{B}S_{(r)}}{T_{\mathrm{draft}}+T_{\mathrm{verify}}(N+B)}, (1)

where the numerator counts one guaranteed token per request plus the expected accepted drafts, and the denominator is the profiled step latency. Since survival only shrinks along a draft, the selection is always a prefix of each draft (A,B,D, dropping E), which verification requires. AdaFlash similarly truncates verification based on a predicted acceptance ratio (Qian et al., 2026). Adaptive verification, however, still drafts all KK tokens before deciding how many to verify.

4 Motivational Study

Drafter overhead under adaptive verification. Adaptive verification shrinks the target’s verification work under load, but the drafter still produces all KK tokens for every request, so drafting grows to up to 40% of step time (Fig. 1(b)). This also limits the adoption of a larger KK, which typically yields longer acceptance (Chen et al., 2026a) but further raises drafting cost under load (Appendix G). Borrowing draft-length control from prior work appears to be a natural fix, but two challenges stand in the way.

Draft length cannot be adjusted during drafting. Unlike an autoregressive drafter, which can stop once its confidence drops (Huang et al., 2025a), a parallel drafter produces all KK tokens in one pass, so it must fix its length before any draft token or confidence exists. The length must therefore be estimated beforehand, and prior work uses past acceptance for this (Li et al., 2026a). Past acceptance is a poor proxy (Pan et al., 2025), as the accepted count changes between consecutive steps in over 80% of cases and by three or more tokens in about 40% (Fig. 3(a)). Adaptive verification also hides it, since tokens beyond the verified prefix are never scored, so a history-based controller that shortens a draft observes only shorter acceptance and may keep shrinking it. A load-aware, batch-wise KK (Fig. 1(a), BW) avoids estimation, but acceptance varies across requests as well as across steps, so one length for the whole batch cannot follow it.

Joint length allocation is combinatorial yet must be computationally cheap. DSpark’s objective treats drafting latency as a constant (Eq. 1), so it never trades drafted tokens against drafting time. Making each draft length a decision variable couples it with the verification budget, because a token never drafted cannot be verified, and the joint space grows as KnK^{n} for nn requests while the choice must be made at every step. Bidirectional attention adds another complication. For each length dd, Fig. 3(b) shows that 4–38% of dd-token drafts differ in at least one token from the first dd tokens of the 15-token draft, so a shorter draft is a different proposal rather than a truncation. Thus, a scheduler should consider every draft length (d≤Kd\leq K) separately.11 1 Although these differences are large, on the DFlash2 backbone a single length-KK curve predicts acceptance as accurately as per-length estimates (Section 7.4). ForeSpark still handles the general case at a similar cost for drafters where this may not hold.

These observations motivate work-conserving speculation, which estimates per-length acceptance before drafting and allocates draft and verification lengths jointly per request.

5 ForeSpark: Realizing Work-Conserving Speculation

ForeSpark realizes work-conserving speculation by deciding how much to draft before any drafting cost is paid. As Fig. 4(a,b) contrasts, DSpark drafts a full block and drops unpromising drafts only at verification, whereas ForeSpark sizes each draft beforehand, so far fewer drafted tokens go unverified. Fig. 4(c) maps the four stages of WCS onto ForeSpark system components. Pre-draft estimate. The pre-draft estimator predicts each request’s acceptance at every candidate length (Section 5.2). Joint schedule. The ForeSpark-Scheduler turns these predictions into a per-request draft schedule 𝐃=(d1,…,dn)\mathbf{D}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}) and a verification budget BB (Section 5.3). Draft. The variable-length drafter executes 𝐃\mathbf{D}. Distribute. The post-draft estimator re-scores the drafted tokens, and the budget distributor allocates BB to the most promising ones (Section 5.4). Because only the total budget BB is fixed before drafting, ForeSpark distributes it per request using the actually realized drafts. Leaving this distribution to the GPU also reduces host-GPU synchronization (Section 6).

5.1 Preliminaries: Parallel Drafting Backbone

We build on DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), which forms the drafter in Fig. 4(c), because it attains acceptance lengths similar to DSpark (Section 7.6) while replacing the sequential corrector with a lightweight path selector over the backbone’s top candidates. Following EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025), the drafter conditions on the target model’s hidden states from several intermediate layers. A learned projection fuses those hidden states into context features Hfeat∈ℝT×dhH_{\mathrm{feat}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{h}}, one vector for each of the TT tokens in the target’s context, where dhd_{h} is the drafter’s hidden dimension. For request ii, a length-dd draft takes as input the embedding of the anchor token followed by dd learned mask embeddings, one for each draft position j=1,…,dj=1,\ldots,d, similar to Fig. 2. Each draft layer attends bidirectionally to all draft positions and to HfeatH_{\mathrm{feat}}, which enters only as additional keys and values. The last layer yields a hidden state hi,jh_{i,j} for each draft position jj, and the LM head turns it into the proposed token xi,jx_{i,j}.

5.2 Context-Aware Pre-Draft Estimation

As Fig. 5 shows, the pre-draft survival estimator predicts, before drafting, how every candidate draft length would perform for each request. Instead of past acceptance (Section 4), it reads two inputs from the verification pass that just finished, both describing what comes next: the context feature ci=Hfeat​[ai]c_{i}=H_{\mathrm{feat}}[a_{i}], the row of HfeatH_{\mathrm{feat}} at the anchor’s position aia_{i} in the context, and the anchor token’s embedding eie_{i}. Since a length-dd draft need not be the prefix of a longer one, the estimator predicts a separate survival curve for every candidate length. To stay computationally cheap on the critical path between verification and drafting, it fuses the inputs in a low-rank space of dimension r≪dhr\ll d_{h} (rr=256 by default) with one hidden layer,

ui\displaystyle u_{i} =SiLU⁡(Wc​ci+We​ei)∈ℝr,\displaystyle=\operatorname{SiLU}\left(W_{c}c_{i}+W_{e}e_{i}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, (2)
zi\displaystyle z_{i} =Wo​ui∈ℝK⁡(K+1)/2,\displaystyle=W_{o}u_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K(K+1)/2},

where WcW_{c} and WeW_{e} project cic_{i} and eie_{i} into a shared rr-dimensional hidden representation uiu_{i}, and WoW_{o} maps uiu_{i} to the K⁡(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2 conditional-acceptance logits, with biases omitted for clarity. Applying SiLU to Wc​ci+We​eiW_{c}c_{i}+W_{e}e_{i} fuses the two inputs nonlinearly, and WoW_{o} reads every candidate length from uiu_{i}. As cic_{i} and eie_{i} are already rich target representations, a single hidden layer suffices, and the estimator costs only a few matrix-vector products per request.

As depicted in Fig. 5, the output forms a triangle whose row zi(d)∈ℝdz_{i}^{(d)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} describes a length-dd draft, with entry zi,t(d)z_{i,t}^{(d)} being the conditional-acceptance logit of position tt, and the running product of their sigmoids gives the survival benefit

Si,d,j=∏t=1jσ⁡(zi,t(d))≈Pr⁡(Ai,d≥j),S_{i,d,j}=\prod_{t=1}^{j}\sigma\big(z_{i,t}^{(d)}\big)\approx\Pr\!\left(A_{i,d}\geq j\right), (3)

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function and Ai,dA_{i,d} is the number of accepted tokens when request ii drafts dd tokens. Verifying the first b≤db\leq d tokens of a length-dd draft is then expected to yield Rewardi​(d,b)=∑j=1bSi,d,j\mathrm{Reward}_{i}(d,b)=\sum_{j=1}^{b}S_{i,d,j} accepted tokens, so the length-3 draft in Fig. 5 with benefits 0.9,0.7,0.30.9,0.7,0.3 gives Rewardi​(3,3)=1.9\mathrm{Reward}_{i}(3,3)=1.9. The estimator predicts per-position acceptance rather than the scheduler’s survival scores (Section 5.3), since verification already labels acceptance for training (Section 5.5). For a directional drafter, i.e., one with causal attention within the block, shorter drafts are exact prefixes of longer ones, so every row equals a prefix of row KK and WoW_{o} needs only KK logits instead of K⁡(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2. ForeSpark also works well for such a drafter (Section 7.5).

5.3 Lightweight Draft-Verify Joint Scheduling

As Fig. 6 shows, the ForeSpark-Scheduler turns per-length rewards into a draft schedule 𝐃\mathbf{D} and a verification budget BB in one pass. Unlike Eq. 1, it prices drafting latency, so it drafts tightly at high load and generously at low load, where extra drafts add little latency. Its search jointly covers every draft length of every request and the verification budget, yet stays computationally cheap as follows.

Per-request reward curve generation. To choose draft lengths, the scheduler values each length-dd draft as if all its tokens were verified, Ri​(d)=Rewardi​(d,d)R_{i}(d)=\mathrm{Reward}_{i}(d,d) with Ri​(0)=0R_{i}(0)=0, and leaves how many tokens to verify to the joint schedule later. A longer draft may lift the yield of its earlier positions (Fig. 6, RiR_{i} plot), so RiR_{i} need not be concave, and a greedy rule that extends a draft only while the next token pays off could stop early and lose the larger gain of a longer draft.

Concave envelope and survival score generation. Therefore, as shown in Fig. 6, the scheduler replaces RiR_{i} with its upper concave envelope FiF_{i}, the smallest concave function above RiR_{i} on {0,…,K}\{0,\ldots,K\}, and defines the survival score gi,d=Fi​(d)−Fi​(d−1)g_{i,d}=F_{i}(d)-F_{i}(d-1), the marginal gain of drafting the dd-th token. By concavity, the scores gi,dg_{i,d} are non-increasing in dd, which the next stage relies on. Where an extra token alone pays off little but enables a larger gain later, FiF_{i} spreads that gain evenly over the tokens in between, so the selection does not stop early. Building the envelope takes O⁡(K)O(K) time and leaves a concave RiR_{i} unchanged.

Global survival score gather. As DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) does in adaptive verification, the scheduler pools all requests’ scores and sorts them, g(1)≥g(2)≥⋯g_{(1)}\geq g_{(2)}\geq\cdots, where g(r)g_{(r)} is the rr-th largest. Because each request’s scores are non-increasing, the top entries form a prefix of every request and directly yield a valid schedule 𝐃\mathbf{D} in the next step (i.e., the joint schedule). This selection maximizes ∑iFi​(di)\sum_{i}F_{i}(d_{i}) without searching KnK^{n} schedules, averaging within 0.01% of the optimum on real batches (Section 7.4).

Joint schedule. Finally, the scheduler chooses 𝐃\mathbf{D} and BB, verifying no more than it drafts,

(𝐃,B)=arg​max𝐃,B≤∑idi⁡n+∑r=1Bg(r)Tdraft​(𝐃)+Tverify​(N+B),(\mathbf{D},B)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{D},\,B\leq\sum_{i}d_{i}}\frac{n+\sum_{r=1}^{B}g_{(r)}}{T_{\mathrm{draft}}(\mathbf{D})+T_{\mathrm{verify}}(N+B)}, (4)

where the numerator counts one token per request plus the expected accepted drafts among the top-BB positions, and the denominator is the offline-profiled step latency. Since the scheduler fixes only the total BB, which may stay below ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i}, it can over-draft and leave the per-request verification split to the post-draft stage (Section 5.4). The search is computationally cheap as the drafter and target model replay CUDA graphs for a few token-count buckets, so each latency is constant within a bucket. Within each pair of buckets, the largest feasible schedule is best, so the scheduler checks one candidate per pair, reducing Eq. 4 to a small grid.

5.4 Draft and Distribute: Variable-Length Drafting and Post-Draft Budget Distribution

Once the drafts exist, the post-draft estimator can use information the pre-draft estimator never had (Fig. 7). The pre-draft estimator decides how much drafting compute to commit, while the post-draft estimator sees the realized tokens and decides where the verification budget is best spent, which is what makes over-drafting worthwhile.

Per-request variable-length drafting. ForeSpark packs the blocks of all requests, each with its anchor and did_{i} masks, into one flat batch with block-diagonal attention, so drafter compute scales with ∑i(di+1)\sum_{i}(d_{i}+1) rather than n⁡(K+1)n(K+1), and shorter drafts actually reduce drafting cost. In Fig. 7, the fourth mask is dropped before the backbone runs, so it executes exactly the length the scheduler priced.

Post-draft survival estimation. DFlash2’s path selector keeps a few candidate tokens per position from the backbone and picks one by conditioning on the token chosen at the previous position (Inco AI, 2026), replacing C with D in the example. The hidden state hi,jh_{i,j} therefore reflects the backbone’s belief before this choice, not the token xi,jx_{i,j} actually proposed. Similar to the confidence head of DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), which pairs the backbone hidden state with an embedding of the previous token, the post-draft estimator pairs hi,jh_{i,j} with a selector feature si,j=(Ws​hi,j)⊙Epred​(xi,j−1)s_{i,j}=(W_{s}h_{i,j})\odot E_{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{i,j-1}), where WsW_{s} is a learned projection, EpredE_{\mathrm{pred}} the selector’s embedding of the previous token xi,j−1x_{i,j-1}, and ⊙\odot the elementwise product,

pi,j=σ⁡(w⊤​[hi,j;si,j]),S^i,j=∏t=1jpi,t,p_{i,j}=\sigma\left(w^{\top}[h_{i,j};s_{i,j}]\right),\qquad\widehat{S}_{i,j}=\prod_{t=1}^{j}p_{i,t}, (5)

where ww is a learned weight vector (bias omitted) and [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] concatenation. Here pi,jp_{i,j} estimates the probability of accepting token jj given its predecessors, and S^i,j\widehat{S}_{i,j} is its post-draft survival probability. One linear layer suffices, as hi,jh_{i,j} and si,js_{i,j} already carry rich backbone and selector information.

Budget distribution. The budget distributor selects the top-BB positions by S^i,j\widehat{S}_{i,j} across the batch, applying DSpark’s adaptive verification (Cheng et al., 2026) (Section 3) to ForeSpark’s variable-length drafts. The target verifies these BB tokens with the NN non-speculative ones as one packed batch. As S^i,j\widehat{S}_{i,j} never increases in jj, the selection forms a prefix of each draft. This prefix is fixed before verification, which applies standard speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2023), so the output distribution is unchanged.

5.5 Training and Calibration

Both estimators are trained jointly with the DFlash2 drafter by adding their losses to its objective, ℒ=ℒDFlash2+λpre​ℒpre+λpost​ℒpost\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DFlash2}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pre}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{post}}. Instead of a binary label of whether each draft token was accepted, they learn from a soft acceptance target, the probability that the token would be accepted, which gives a smoother training signal. Following DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), the target for position jj is its acceptance probability under speculative sampling, αj=∑v∈𝒞jmin⁡{Pj​(v),Qj​(v)}\alpha_{j}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}_{j}}\min\{P_{j}(v),Q_{j}(v)\}, with the target distribution PjP_{j} and the drafter’s proposal QjQ_{j}. Unlike DSpark, the sum covers only 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j}, the candidate tokens the path selector keeps, and QjQ_{j} is the proposal over them after the selector’s choice. For the pre-draft estimator, each training step samples a length dd, runs the backbone at exactly that length, and trains row z(d)z^{(d)} on that length’s targets αd,j\alpha_{d,j} with binary cross-entropy, since bidirectional drafts of different lengths differ. Gradients stop at cic_{i} and eie_{i}, so this loss trains only the pre-draft estimator and leaves the drafter unchanged. The post-draft estimator is trained against αj\alpha_{j} with a weighted binary cross-entropy that excludes the anchor. Since each survival estimate multiplies the per-position probabilities, a small error at each position accumulates along the draft. After training, we therefore recalibrate both estimators on Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) prompts, fitting a temperature for each position of the post-draft estimator, as in DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), and fitting a scale and bias for each entry of the pre-draft estimator (see Appendix B).

6 Implementation

We implement ForeSpark on vLLM 0.30.0 (Kwon et al., 2023) with about 4K lines of Python and Triton, and train the drafters and estimators with Speculators (Red Hat, 2025).

Scheduler optimization. ForeSpark splits the scheduler so that the host never waits on the GPU: the host decides how many tokens to draft and verify, the GPU decides which ones, and the two exchange only scores and totals. Before drafting in step tt, the host computes the totals of Eq. 4, ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i} and BB, from the pre-draft scores the GPU copied to it in step t−1t-1, and sends ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i} to the GPU. A newly admitted request without scores on the host uses the others’ mean scores (under 1% of request-steps). The GPU then runs the pre-draft estimator on the current target states, splits ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i} into per-request lengths did_{i} by ranking these fresh scores with a one-pass Triton kernel, and asynchronously copies the scores to the host for step t+1t+1. Meanwhile, the host recomputes BB with the verification step’s actual non-speculative token count NN and sizes that step at N+BN+B tokens. Using this BB, the GPU’s budget distributor then picks the top-BB positions by their post-draft estimates with the same score-ranking Triton kernel.

Execution. Each decoding step replays captured CUDA graphs for the pre-draft estimator, the drafter, and the output stage, which applies the LM head, picks the draft tokens, and runs the post-draft estimator. The drafting and verification latency tables are built by timing these graphs once. Under tensor parallelism, small numerical differences across ranks could produce different schedules and stall collective operations. ForeSpark therefore broadcasts rank 0’s pre-draft scores, draft tokens, post-draft estimates, and acceptance decisions at every step (each at most K⁡(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2 values per request) and uses rank 0’s latency tables, so all ranks schedule from identical inputs.

Hybrid and sparse-attention targets. The sparse-MLA kernels of the GLM models need each request’s lengths on the host before launch. For these targets, the host performs the per-request split and selects the verified positions itself, from the previous step’s estimates, and the GPU executes them. Stale estimates affect only which tokens are drafted and verified, not the output, as verification is lossless.

7 Evaluation

7.1 Experimental Setup

Models. We use models that span dense, mixture-of-experts (MoE), and hybrid architectures with 14–744B parameters: Qwen3-14B (Yang et al., 2025), a 40-layer dense model served in BF16, GLM5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026) (320B, 18B active), a hybrid MoE model whose 45 layers interleave KDA linear attention (Kimi Team et al., 2025) and MLA with DSA sparse attention (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024a; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), and GLM5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026) (744B, 40B active), a 78-layer MoE model using MLA with DSA sparse attention. Models are served with 8-way tensor parallelism (TP8), plus 8-way expert parallelism (EP8) for the MoE models, and both GLM models use NVFP4 routed experts and an FP8 KV cache. We use the lowest reasoning effort and greedy decoding (temperature 0) unless noted.

Hardware and software. We serve Qwen3-14B on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs (96 GB each), and train all drafters and serve GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3 on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs (180 GB each), with vLLM 0.30.0, PyTorch 2.13, and CUDA 13.0 (host details in Appendix C).

Baselines. We compare ForeSpark, which jointly schedules drafting and verification, with autoregressive decoding without speculation (AR) and three parallel-drafting baselines: DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), a recent parallel drafter, which drafts and verifies a full block, Batchwise (BW), DFlash2 with vLLM’s load-based schedule (vLLM Team, 2026), which caps the speculation length of the whole batch at a pre-calibrated value per load, and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), a goodput-aware parallel drafter with adaptive verification. We also evaluate ForeSpark w/o JS, ForeSpark without its pre-draft estimator and joint scheduler (JS), which drafts full blocks and applies adaptive verification with ForeSpark’s post-draft estimator, isolating the gain of joint scheduling. It thus applies the same adaptive verification as DSpark and differs mainly in the drafter backbone. All parallel drafters follow their published training recipes (e.g., 5/6 layers) and use a maximum draft length of KK=15, with KK=7 for sensitivity (Section 7.5). To show that WCS generalizes, we also apply it to DSpark and to two autoregressive drafters with KK=5, MTP (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024b) and EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) (Section 7.7). Drafter training and the pre-deployment calibration details are in Appendices A and B.

Workloads and metrics. Our main workload replays 20,000 multi-turn ShareGPT (anon8231489123, 2023) conversations, and a decode-only variant releases each batch together after prefill and times 512 decode tokens per answer. In closed-loop runs, we sweep the load, the number of active clients and thus the batch size, from one to the largest load each deployment fits (e.g., 512 on Qwen3-14B) and plot total output tokens per second (TPS) against user interactivity, the per-user TPS given by the inverse of the median time per output token (TPOT, excluding the first token). We compare methods at matched user interactivity as in DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), interpolating between measured points and reporting only points where a method reaches at least half of its peak throughput. In open-loop runs, requests arrive as a seeded Poisson process, and following Li et al. (2023), we report service level objective (SLO) attainment, the fraction of requests meeting both their time to first token (TTFT) and TPOT targets, and capacity, the arrival rate at which attainment falls to 90% (Appendix C).

7.2 Analysis on Serving Performance

On the decode-only (ShareGPT-Decode) and end-to-end (ShareGPT-E2E) workloads of Fig. 8, ForeSpark achieves up to 1.31/1.40/1.34×\times and 1.34/1.21/1.18×\times the throughput of the strongest baseline at matched user interactivity (arrows) and 1.77/1.40/1.34×\times and 1.53/1.21/1.18×\times that of DSpark on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3. The gains reach 1.37/1.46/1.46×\times and 1.43/1.24/1.30×\times over ForeSpark w/o JS, which shares ForeSpark’s backbone, and 1.61/2.49/2.39×\times and 2.04/2.19/2.08×\times over AR.

Adaptive verification lets DSpark and ForeSpark w/o JS outperform DFlash2 under high load, but both still draft every block in full and pay the drafter overhead. ForeSpark reduces this overhead with joint scheduling and outperforms both. The gains of ForeSpark over DSpark are larger on ShareGPT-Decode, since in ShareGPT-E2E prefill tokens share each step with decoding and add non-speculative tokens NN that draft scheduling does not reduce. BW even outperforms DSpark at several loads, showing that its load-based cap is effective there. However, it applies one length to the batch regardless of each request’s acceptance, whereas ForeSpark schedules drafts per request and outperforms it.

At a load (batch size) of one, where full-block drafting is preferable and lies within ForeSpark’s design space, ForeSpark attains 1.15/1.07/0.96×\times and 1.11/0.98/0.98×\times the user interactivity of DSpark on ShareGPT-Decode and ShareGPT-E2E, with the small gap on GLM5.3 consistent with DSpark’s slightly higher acceptance (Section 7.6). On Qwen3-14B ShareGPT-Decode, AR has the highest throughput at the heaviest load, where verification is compute-bound, but ForeSpark comes closest among speculative methods and surpasses AR at higher user interactivity. On Qwen3-14B ShareGPT-E2E, in contrast, ForeSpark exceeds AR even at the heaviest load. We attribute this to long multi-turn chat histories in ShareGPT-E2E, which keep every method memory-bound, so extra verification stays computationally cheap and speculation remains worthwhile.

SLO attainment. Open-loop runs use the end-to-end workload, as a decode-only run cannot measure TTFT. At 90% attainment (Fig. 9(a)), ForeSpark sustains 1.20/1.13/1.17×\times the request rate of the strongest baseline, 1.51/1.13/1.17×\times that of DSpark, and 1.29/1.13/1.28×\times that of ForeSpark w/o JS on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3. Once requests queue, extra step time delays active generations and queued prefills, so reducing unproductive drafting and verification keeps both SLOs met at higher rates.

Fig. 9(b) fixes the request rate just above DSpark’s capacity (33/23/16 requests/s) and scales the TTFT and TPOT thresholds by a common factor. At the original thresholds, ForeSpark meets the SLOs for 100/100/95% of requests, against 17/53/7% for DSpark and 100/43/4% for ForeSpark w/o JS. ForeSpark keeps attainment above 90% even when the thresholds are tightened to 0.2/0.8/1.0×\times, whereas DSpark stays below 90% even when they are relaxed to 2×\times on Qwen3-14B and GLM5.3-Flash and 4×\times on GLM5.3. At this rate, DSpark’s queue keeps growing, so looser thresholds recover only a fraction of its requests, while ForeSpark still has headroom.

7.3 Execution Time Breakdown Analysis

Fig. 10 breaks down the time per output token. At the largest batch size, ForeSpark reduces drafting time by 76/68/67% relative to DSpark on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3, as it packs only the scheduled draft positions (Section 5.4), and by 62/70/76% even against ForeSpark w/o JS, which shares the same backbone, so the saving comes from joint scheduling rather than the backbone. Joint scheduling cuts drafts from 15 to 2.04/4.75/3.55 tokens per request at the largest batch size, and ForeSpark verifies nearly all of them (Appendix D). Total time drops by 37/13/11% relative to DSpark, and on Qwen3-14B, DSpark and ForeSpark w/o JS need 1.41×\times and 1.14×\times AR’s time per token, whereas ForeSpark needs 0.89×\times. Verification time also drops at some batch sizes (e.g., 12% at 128 requests on GLM5.3-Flash) despite the same post-draft estimator as ForeSpark w/o JS, which we attribute to joint scheduling sizing drafts and verification together.

7.4 Analysis on Joint Scheduler

On GLM5.3-Flash with a common DFlash2 backbone (Fig. 11(a)), adaptive verification alone (+AV, i.e., ForeSpark w/o JS) improves throughput by up to 1.56×\times over full verification (DFlash2), and joint scheduling adds up to 1.17×\times on top. This gain relies on a computationally cheap search, as an exhaustive scheduler with the same inputs (Exhaustive) falls below +AV at batch sizes of 64 and 192 and trails ForeSpark by up to 1.22×\times. ForeSpark decides a schedule in 88 μ\mus at 192 requests, against 8.2 ms for Exhaustive, used only as an optimality reference, with an average goodput loss of at most 0.01% (Fig. 11(b)).

ForeSpark-SC (single curve) replaces the per-length estimator with one shared length-KK curve, which assumes prefix structure and makes each RiR_{i} concave. Despite the token differences in Section 4, it predicts acceptance as accurately and matches ForeSpark in all panels, so the backbone admits this simpler form, which ForeSpark forgoes for generality.

7.5 Sensitivity Studies

Dataset. ForeSpark’s advantage carries over to math and code workloads, with up to 1.49/1.38/1.24×\times the throughput of DSpark on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3 (Appendix E), as it sets each request’s draft length from its current context rather than from a workload-specific setting.

Predictor quality. Although the previous step’s acceptance is infeasible under adaptive verification (Section 4), we compare against it over 1.48M full-block drafts of Qwen3-14B (KK=15, no adaptive verification), where ForeSpark predicts acceptance within one token for 60% of drafts versus 41%, and lowers the mean absolute error from 2.80 to 1.82 tokens (Fig. 12(a)), so the target model’s current features forecast the upcoming draft better than historical acceptance.

Drafter type. With a directional drafter, i.e., causal attention within the block (Fig. 12(b)), ForeSpark still improves throughput over DSpark by up to 1.55×\times at matched user interactivity. Full-block drafting remains overhead under load even for this drafter, which joint scheduling reduces.

Temperature. With temperature 1.0 on Qwen3-14B ShareGPT-E2E (Fig. 12(c)), ForeSpark achieves up to 1.39×\times the throughput of the strongest baseline (BW), 1.76×\times that of DSpark, and 1.70×\times that of AR, compared with 1.34/1.53/2.04×\times under greedy decoding. Sampling lowers acceptance, which narrows the margin over AR but widens the gap to the speculative baselines, as full-block drafting wastes more work when fewer drafts are accepted.

Draft length. With KK=7, ForeSpark achieves up to 1.32×\times the throughput of DSpark on Qwen3-14B and up to 1.24/1.16×\times that of the strongest baseline on GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3, so its gains hold although a smaller KK leaves less drafter work to avoid. A larger KK gives ForeSpark more choices while joint scheduling limits the extra drafting, easing the barrier noted in Section 4. On math and code with Qwen3-14B, KK=15 helps at low load, but at high load it lowers every speculative baseline’s throughput below its KK=7 version. ForeSpark keeps the low-load gain and still achieves the highest throughput at high load (Appendix G).

7.6 Analysis on Acceptance Length and Overhead

Fig. 16 (Appendix F) tests whether ForeSpark’s gains stem from a stronger or more expensive drafter. At KK=15 without adaptive verification, ForeSpark reaches mean acceptance lengths of 4.38/3.33/3.37 on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3 over SPEED-Bench’s 11 categories (Abramovich et al., 2026), within 3.2% of DSpark and equal to DFlash2 since its estimators only score drafts from the same backbone, so the serving gains do not rely on higher acceptance. Training costs little extra, taking 1.12/1.05/1.11×\times the time per iteration of DSpark and only 3–5% more than DFlash2, since length sampling trains one pre-draft row per step instead of running the drafter at every length (Section 5.5). The pre-/post-draft estimators add only 0.1–0.2% parameters, and the drafter is 3.7–5.0% larger than DSpark’s due to the DFlash2 backbone.

7.7 Analysis on WCS with Other Drafters

Since WCS needs only a drafter latency profile and a pre-draft estimator on the target’s context feature and anchor embedding (Section 5.2), it is not tied to ForeSpark’s drafter, and Fig. 13 applies it to the parallel drafter DSpark and the autoregressive drafters MTP and EAGLE-3, keeping each drafter’s maximum draft length and serving the same checkpoint with and without WCS. At matched user interactivity, WCS improves throughput by up to 1.27/1.30/1.26×\times over DSpark, MTP, and EAGLE-3 (see Appendix H for implementation details).

8 Discussion

Where ForeSpark helps most. Since full-block drafting is one of its schedules, ForeSpark stays comparable to DSpark at low load while extending speculative decoding to higher loads and decode-dominated workloads, where speculation is usually considered unsuitable (Sections 7.2 and 7.3).

Remaining headroom. Against an oracle that knows each draft’s acceptance, both pre-/post-draft estimators remain conservative. This partly stems from our calibration on the external Alpaca dataset, which assumes an unknown workload. Further gains thus lie in workload-matched calibration or better workload-adaptive estimators.

Fairness. Global sorting may leave a request undrafted in a step, which never changes outputs but can skew per-request speedups. Per-request minimum budgets could fix this.

9 Related Work

Goodput-aware speculation in LLM serving. Complementary to drafter designs (Appendix I), serving systems schedule prefill and decoding for throughput or goodput (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024), but under load extra verification competes with other requests and can reduce or even reverse the benefit of speculation (Su et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2026c). To address this, TurboSpec (Liu et al., 2024b) and Nightjar (Li et al., 2026b) choose one speculation length per batch, and AdaServe (Li et al., 2026c), AdaSpec (Huang et al., 2025b), FASER (Chen et al., 2026c), and ECHO (Hu et al., 2026b) size it per request or tree, often under SLO or budget constraints, mostly for autoregressive or tree drafters. Verification budgeting selects the most promising draft tokens across requests (Wu et al., 2025), including for parallel drafters (Cheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b; Qian et al., 2026), but only after a full block is drafted, leaving the drafter overhead.

Draft length control. Adaptive draft lengths are mostly studied for autoregressive drafters through learned stopping predictors (Huang et al., 2025a; Mamou et al., 2024), single-request length regression (Zhang et al., 2024), drafting overlapped with verification (Liu et al., 2025), tree search (Wang et al., 2025), or online tuning (Hou et al., 2025). For parallel drafters, DiffuSpec (Li et al., 2026a) sizes drafts from recent acceptance, FailFast (Pan et al., 2025) and DLoop (Gu et al., 2026) keep drafting while confident at the cost of extra passes, and TreeSpark (Zhou et al., 2026) prunes a draft tree by path survival and shrinks it under load but builds it from a full backbone pass. None of them sizes each request’s draft before a parallel drafter’s pass from current-context acceptance estimates, jointly with a verification budget.

10 Conclusion

We presented WCS and its prototype ForeSpark, which estimate acceptance before drafting, jointly allocate per-request draft lengths and the verification budget, and spend it with post-draft confidence, improving throughput by up to 1.77×\times over DSpark. We hope WCS guides how future parallel drafters are designed and scheduled for LLM serving.

AI Usage Disclosure

We used Anthropic’s Claude models (e.g., Opus 5.5) as an assistant in parts of this work. All research ideas, design decisions, and conclusions are the authors’ own, and the authors reviewed and verified every AI-assisted output.

Ideation and motivation. The research problem, the motivational observations, and the design of work-conserving speculation are the authors’ own, and the motivational measurements were designed and run by the authors.

Literature search. We used the assistant to search for related work and to check whether our idea had been proposed before. The authors read the identified papers themselves, and every citation was verified against its primary source.

Code. The authors implemented ForeSpark with AI assistance for code generation, most notably to optimize the Triton kernel for variable-length drafting. All AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested by the authors.

Experiment design and data. The authors designed and ran all experiments, using the assistant for feedback in discussion and to write plotting scripts. No benchmark or evaluation data were generated with AI tools.

Writing. The authors wrote the content of the paper. Under the authors’ direction, the assistant was used to revise drafts for clarity and concision and to check consistency between the text, figures, and notation. The authors checked and substantially revised all AI-assisted text and take full responsibility for the content.

Appendix A Drafter Training Details

Training. We train all drafters with Speculators (Red Hat, 2025) on 958K user turns from Magpie (Xu et al., 2025) and UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023), after removing the SPEED-Bench (Abramovich et al., 2026) prompts. To generate training data, the target model regenerates every response with its recommended sampling settings, up to 8,192 tokens, with thinking disabled on Qwen3-14B and the lowest reasoning effort on the GLM models. During training, a vLLM server running the target supplies the hidden states of the captured layers (Table 1). A trainer trains the parallel drafters on the regenerated data, using KK=15 with bidirectional attention within the block and 8,192-token sequences with up to 3,072 anchors. Their loss is 0.1 times cross-entropy plus 0.9 times total variation, with position weights that decay exponentially. We train for three epochs with AdamW and a cosine schedule at the learning rates of the published recipes (6×10−46\times 10^{-4} for DFlash2 and 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} for DSpark). DFlash2, BW, and ForeSpark w/o JS use ForeSpark’s backbone, so DFlash2 drafts the same tokens as ForeSpark at length KK. For other drafter hyperparameters, such as the number of layers and the captured target layers, we use the settings of widely adopted published drafters.

Pre-draft labels. The training length dd of Section 5.5 cycles through K,1,…,K−1K,1,\ldots,K-1 across steps. When d<Kd<K, the drafter first re-drafts at length dd from every fourth anchor without gradients, and the labels αd,j\alpha_{d,j} compare only these drafted positions with the target distributions of the step.

Other drafters. The directional drafters of Fig. 12(b) are retrained with causal attention within the block. EAGLE-3 is a one-layer drafter trained with the Speculators recipe for three epochs, and MTP is GLM5.3-Flash’s own multi-token-prediction layer (Appendix H).

Appendix B Calibration Details

After training, we calibrate both pre-/post-draft estimators once per model with their weights fixed, using up to 4,000 Alpaca prompts (Taori et al., 2023) that appear in neither the training data nor any benchmark. The calibration runs use greedy decoding and verify every drafted position, so every position has an acceptance label.

Post-draft estimator. Let ℓi,j=w⊤​[hi,j;si,j]\ell_{i,j}=w^{\top}[h_{i,j};s_{i,j}] be the logit of the post-draft estimator (Section 5.4). Following DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), each position jj gets a temperature θj\theta_{j}, so that pi,j=σ⁡(ℓi,j/θj)p_{i,j}=\sigma(\ell_{i,j}/\theta_{j}) and S^i,j=∏t≤jpi,t\widehat{S}_{i,j}=\prod_{t\leq j}p_{i,t}. The temperatures are fitted in order from jj=1 to KK, as

θj=arg​minθ∈ΘECE(S^i,j(θ), 1[Ai,K≥j]),\theta_{j}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}\operatorname{ECE}\bigl(\widehat{S}_{i,j}(\theta),\,\mathbf{1}[A_{i,K}\geq j]\bigr), (6)

where S^i,j​(θ)\widehat{S}_{i,j}(\theta) uses θ\theta at position jj and the already fitted temperatures before it, Ai,KA_{i,K} is the number of accepted tokens when request ii drafts the full length KK (Section 5.2), ECE is the expected calibration error over 15 equal-width bins, and the grid Θ\Theta holds 41 values evenly spaced in log⁡θ\log\theta from 0.1 to 10. The traces come from 1,000 of the prompts, drafted at the full length KK with up to 256 output tokens each at a load of 16. DSpark is calibrated in the same way, and the temperature-1.0 runs reuse the greedy fit.

Pre-draft estimator. Since each draft length yields a distinct proposal, we calibrate each entry (d,j)(d,j) of the triangle in Section 5.2 on a run at exactly length dd. The calibrated conditional acceptance is σ⁡(ad,j​zi,j(d)+bd,j)\sigma(a_{d,j}z^{(d)}_{i,j}+b_{d,j}), where the scale ad,ja_{d,j} and bias bd,jb_{d,j} come from a logistic regression of whether position jj is accepted, fitted on the drafts whose first j−1j-1 tokens are accepted. One run per length d=1,…,15d=1,\ldots,15 on the 4,000 prompts, sweeping the load up to 512 requests (256 on GLM5.3), yields all K⁡(K+1)/2K(K+1)/2 pairs. A directional drafter needs only the length-KK run, since its shorter drafts are prefixes of the longer one.

Latency tables and BW. ForeSpark takes drafting latencies from its startup profile (Section 6) and verification latencies from offline profiles. Each verification entry is the median target forward time for a given batch size and number of verified tokens per request, over at least 30 decode-only steps. For the length cap of BW in vLLM 0.30, we run every cap k=1,…,15k=1,\ldots,15 at every load on the 4,000 prompts and assign each load range its fastest cap.

Appendix C Evaluation Workload and Metric Details

The Qwen3-14B server has two Intel Xeon Platinum 8480CL CPUs and the B200 servers have two AMD EPYC 9654 CPUs, each with 2 TB of DDR5 DRAM. Each method runs alone on the node with the settings of Table 1.

ShareGPT-E2E. We take the first 20,000 ShareGPT conversations with at least four turns and form a stream of 88,051 requests, one per user turn. Each request carries the conversation so far, up to about 16K tokens, and consecutive turns of a conversation are about 512 requests apart. A request ends at the end-of-turn token or after 4,096 output tokens. Each closed-loop point starts from an empty prefix cache and warms up on held-out conversations for at least 30 s, until the batch reaches 90% of the load or stops growing. It then measures at least 128 requests over at least 120 s, and every method replays the same request sequence. We compare methods at matched user interactivity as in DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026). We interpolate each curve linearly in log user interactivity between adjacent loads and report ratios only where both methods run at no less than half of their peak throughput.

ShareGPT-Decode. Each batch of CC requests, where CC is the batch size, is prefilled from an empty prefix cache and held at an engine-side barrier until every request has its first token, and then all requests are released together. Each request is timed over the 512 tokens after its first token, cut at its first end-of-turn token (e.g., <|im_end|> on Qwen3-14B). To keep such cuts rare, we first decode the 4,096 ShareGPT prompts closest to 1K characters greedily with AR and keep only those whose answer reaches 641 tokens (1,572/618/646 prompts on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3). Since verification is lossless, every method then times the same answers, and only 2% of the timed answers on Qwen3-14B still end early, because numerical differences can change the greedy choice between nearly tied tokens. A batch’s throughput is the sum of its requests’ token rates over their timed spans, and its user interactivity is the median of these rates.

Open-loop tests for SLO experiments. Requests arrive as a seeded Poisson process that is identical for every method. At rate rr, 30​r30r warm-up arrivals precede 120​r120r measured ones, and requests that fail or do not finish count as SLO misses. All methods run at the same request rates, chosen from short pilot runs. The sweep uses at most 12 rates: two light-load rates, then evenly spaced rates up to just past the point where ForeSpark, the method with the highest capacity, meets the SLOs for fewer than half of the requests.

Breakdown and acceptance. Fig. 10 normalizes each method’s time per output token to AR, i.e., AR’s throughput divided by the method’s. It splits it into verification, drafting, and other time in proportion to step times from vLLM’s CUDA-event step timer, which costs about 0.03% of wall time. We measure acceptance length, one plus the accepted draft tokens per verification step, on SPEED-Bench’s 880 qualitative prompts (Abramovich et al., 2026) at a load of 32, verifying every drafted token at KK=15.

Appendix D Number of Drafted and Verified Tokens with Joint Scheduling

Fig. 14 counts how many tokens each method drafts, verifies, and accepts per request in each step of Fig. 10, showing how the time breakdown follows the scheduled lengths. DSpark and ForeSpark w/o JS always draft the full block of 15 tokens, but from 32 requests on, adaptive verification keeps only 3.26–4.77 of them and discards the remaining 68–78% of the drafter’s output unverified. ForeSpark drafts only 2.04–5.76 tokens per request at these batch sizes and verifies 99.7–100% of them, which explains its lower drafting time in Section 7.3. ForeSpark verifies between 1.75 fewer and 1.21 more tokens per request than DSpark, since joint scheduling balances drafting and verification rather than shrinking both. At a load of one, ForeSpark drafts 14.71/9.72/7.00 tokens per request, and on GLM5.3-Flash and GLM5.3, it over-drafts, leaving 3.67/0.87 for the post-draft stage to drop (Section 5.3).

Appendix E Dataset Sensitivity: Math and Code Workload

To show that ForeSpark’s advantages are not tied to one workload, we also evaluate it on a math and code workload in Fig. 15. The workload draws 2,855 single-turn prompts from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), AIME25 (Zhang and Math-AI Team, 2025), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025) v5–v6, each with its set’s usual instruction. It runs in closed loop like ShareGPT-E2E, with the prefix cache disabled. At matched user interactivity, ForeSpark reaches up to 1.49/1.38/1.24×\times the throughput of DSpark and up to 1.29/1.38/1.24×\times that of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3 (arrows in Fig. 15). These answers are more predictable than ShareGPT’s (Table 3), so ForeSpark outperforms AR at every load, unlike on Qwen3-14B ShareGPT-Decode (Section 7.2). As on ShareGPT, the gains appear at high load, where ForeSpark shortens drafts of requests with low expected acceptance and keeps long drafts for the rest. The curves converge at high user interactivity, where full-block drafting is preferred and within ForeSpark’s design space.

Appendix F Acceptance Length / Drafter Cost

To show that the serving gains of ForeSpark come from joint scheduling rather than from a stronger or more expensive drafter, we analyze the acceptance lengths of the drafters in Table 2. We use SPEED-Bench’s qualitative split, which covers 11 categories (Abramovich et al., 2026). ForeSpark reaches average acceptance lengths of 4.38/3.33/3.37 on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3, against 4.28/3.35/3.48 for DSpark, staying within 3.2% of DSpark. ForeSpark and DFlash2 share one backbone and have identical acceptance, because the pre-/post-draft estimators only score drafts and never change the drafted tokens. The serving gains over DFlash2 therefore come from how ForeSpark allocates drafting and verification, and those over DSpark do not rely on a higher token yield per full draft.

Fig. 16(b) reports the training time per iteration, measured in fresh runs at KK=15 with the GPU splits of Table 1 and averaged over minutes 10–15 after the first step. ForeSpark takes 1.45/1.04/1.89 s per iteration, which is 1.12/1.05/1.11×\times that of DSpark (1.30/0.99/1.70 s) and only 3–5% more than DFlash2 (1.40/1.01/1.80 s). This overhead stays small because length sampling trains only one row of the pre-draft estimator per step, rather than running the drafter for every candidate length (Section 5.5). With the training steps of Table 1 (112K/154K/162K over three epochs), ForeSpark’s training takes about 45/44/85 hours on eight B200 GPUs, against 44/43/81 hours for DFlash2.

Fig. 16(c) reports drafter parameters, excluding the embedding and LM head that every drafter reuses from the target. ForeSpark has 1.93/1.17/2.46B parameters, almost the same as DFlash2, since the two estimators add only 0.1–0.2%, and 3.7–5.0% more than DSpark (1.86/1.13/2.34B) because of the DFlash2 backbone.

Appendix G Discussion on Draft Length (KK)

Lower KK (KK=7) sensitivity. To demonstrate that ForeSpark still benefits drafters with a smaller KK, we train the drafters with KK=7 using the same recipe. Fig. 17 shows that ForeSpark achieves up to 1.23×\times the decode-only throughput of the strongest baseline, BW, and 1.32×\times that of DSpark at matched user interactivity (Fig. 17(a)). It also sustains 1.21×\times the request rate of DSpark at 90% SLO attainment (42.8 versus 35.5 requests/s, Fig. 17(b)), and at 256 requests it spends 44% less drafting time per output token than DSpark (Fig. 17(c)). On larger models, ForeSpark achieves up to 1.24×\times and 1.16×\times the throughput of the strongest baseline on GLM5.3-Flash and GLM5.3, as shown in Fig. 18(a) and (b). A smaller KK leaves less drafter work to avoid, yet the scheduler still shortens drafts whose expected yield does not justify their cost.

Drafter overhead limits the use of a larger KK. In actual deployment, a larger KK raises acceptance length, but the extra drafter overhead limits its use in LLM serving. Table 3 shows the acceptance gain on math and code, where raising KK from 7 to 15 lengthens ForeSpark’s acceptance by 1.31/1.19/1.17×\times on Qwen3-14B/GLM5.3-Flash/GLM5.3 and DSpark’s by 1.27/1.19/1.13×\times. As shown in Fig. 18(c), KK=15 is preferable at low load, since its higher acceptance translates into higher user interactivity. At higher load, however, every speculative baseline pays the drafter overhead of KK=15 and delivers lower total throughput than its KK=7 counterpart at the same user interactivity.

On the other hand, ForeSpark jointly schedules draft and verification lengths, so it matches the user interactivity of KK=15 at low load and still achieves the highest throughput at high load. This is because ForeSpark drafts a token only when it is expected to pay off, so a larger KK widens its choices while joint scheduling limits the extra drafter work. Thus, the main experiments use KK=15, and ForeSpark lets serving systems benefit from long drafts with reduced drafter overhead under load.

Appendix H WCS with Other Drafters Details

All panels of Fig. 13 run GLM5.3-Flash on ShareGPT-Decode at loads up to 192. WCS on DSpark uses a per-position pre-draft estimator, which assumes a shorter draft is a prefix of a longer one. We therefore retrain DSpark with causal attention within the block and train the estimator alongside it, and both DSpark and DSpark +WCS serve this checkpoint. MTP and EAGLE-3 are autoregressive, so each draft position costs one drafter pass over the whole batch. Shortening only some requests’ drafts saves little time, so WCS instead picks one draft depth per step, up to 5, together with the budget BB, using drafter latencies profiled at each depth. Their pre-draft estimator predicts acceptance at each of the five positions from the target’s hidden state at the last accepted token and the anchor embedding. We train it on a serving log and calibrate it on Alpaca. After drafting, the budget distributor spends BB using vLLM’s online acceptance estimates for these drafters, a per-position logistic model of the drafter’s top-token probability that vLLM refits while serving. In all panels, the gains appear at high load, and the curves converge at low load.

Appendix I Additional Related Work

Parallel speculative decoding. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) has been strengthened with extra decoding heads (Cai et al., 2024), nn-gram drafting (Fu et al., 2024), feature-conditioned autoregressive drafters (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025), tree verification (Miao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), and draft-model distillation (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a). Following blockwise parallel decoding (Stern et al., 2018), parallel drafters propose a block in parallel with diffusion language models (Christopher et al., 2025; Sandler et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a) or in one pass with lightweight drafters (Chen et al., 2026a; An et al., 2026), and later designs restore intra-block dependency (Cheng et al., 2026; Inco AI, 2026; Hu et al., 2026a), build draft trees (Ringel and Romano, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), or distill for higher acceptance (Qian et al., 2026), and these drafter designs can be orthogonal to ForeSpark, which decides how much a given parallel drafter drafts and verifies.
